author: William Makepeace Thackeray
introFa: کتاب «Vanity Fair» نوشته William Makepeace Thackeray یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Vanity Fair»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: VANITY FAIR - A FAIR OF VANITY, OR A FAIR OF CONCEIT, OR O N L Y A WORLD-FAIR? BY K A R I N D O V R I N G It is now one hundred years since William Makepeace Thackeray’s “Vanity Fair” was published for the first time. As is well-known, it was printed serially during the years 1847 and 1848. Presently, “Va- nity Fair” was translated into several other languages, among others into Danish and Swedish. To Frenchmen and other Romanic speaking peoples, the translating of the very striking and suggestive title “Vanity Fair” seems to have offered little difficulty. For example, they have translated it “La foire aux vanitW, as the title was already in the earliest known French edition, in 1855 I). This does not mean, of course, that translators in the Romanic countries caught the exact sense of the title better than those in the non-Romanic countries. Linguistic usage itself does not seem to have given an opportunity of any greater variation of the title. In Germany, however, the translators seem already from the start to have been a little uncertain as to how the title “Vanity Fair” should be interpreted. In the middle of the nineteenth century, Chr. Fr. Grieb translates it “Der Jahrmarkt des Lebens”, and W. E. Drugulin fol- lows him; but A. Diezmann calls his translation “Der Markt des Le- bens”. In 1883, H. Lobedan translates “Vanity Fair” as “Eitelkeits- markt”, whereas Fr. Dobbert, in 1898, returns to the title “Der Jahrmarkt des Lebens”. In 1909, on the other hand, “Vanity Fair” is presented in a German translation as “Der Jahrmarkt der Eitel- I) Translation of Georges Guiffrey, 1 ed. 1855.

VANITY FAIR 77 keit”; after 1920, the translation “Der Jahrmarkt des Lebens” is readopted ). In Norway, translations of Thackeray’s novel were made by Mar- tin Gran 1928-29 and by Margrethe Kjaer in 1937. Both called their translations “Forfengelighetens marked” ’ ). In Denmark, on the other hand, the first translation of “Vanity Fair” was called “Livets 13azar” (“The Bazar of Life”), and was published in 1852. Later on, in 1877-78 and in 1919, A. Damkiaer translated “Vanity Fair” as “Forfaengelighedens Marked” (with the same sense as in Norwegian). In Sweden, the title has been persistently translated - since the earliest translation by N. L. Bolin in 1849 - by the words “FBfln- gans marknad” (“Fair of Conceit”); once (in 1926) the translation is “Vlrldsmarknaden” (“ World-Fair” ). I shall return to these trans- lations later. It may be said, of course, that it is enormously difficult to find the adequate rendering of a book-title in a foreign language. But as, in this case, the question does not only concern the minitiae of trans- lation, but also a problem that is intimately connected with the whole purpose of the novel, it may be of some interest to scrutinize it a little closer. In view of some of the translations of the title quoted above, especially the German and Swedish ones, it is clear that the trans- lators have not quite caught the allusion which Thacheray had in view. The German literary historian Erwin Walter quotes Melville for the well-known circumstances under which Thackeray invented the title “Vanity Fair” for his book. Thackeray had not yet, when he began to write it, thought of the famous title, Melville tells us. The title “Vanity Fair” occurred to Thackeray suddenly in the middle of the night. “1 jumped out of bed, he (i. e. Thackeray) told miss Parry, and ran three times round my room uttering as I went: Vanity Fair! I ) E. 6. Fr. Dobbert: ,Der Jahrmarkt des Lebens (Vanity Fair). Vanity Fair!” ’) But before quoting Melville, Walter cur- sorily mentions, as a sort of well-known fact: “Der Titel ‘Vanity Fair’ selbst, dessen Priigung ja aus Bunyans “The Pilgrim’s Progress” stammt, ist, nach Melville, Thackeray eines Nachts eingefallen, als der Anfang des Werkes schon geschrieben war.” ’) Walter does not adduce any conclusive evidence for his statement. It may, perhaps, seem unnecessary; every reader who is a little familiar with Bunyan’s “The Pilgrim’s Progress” and his description of Vanity Fair, and who has afterwards felt the atmosphere of “Vanitas Vanitatum” that per- vades Thackeray’s novel, will find it identical with the same phrase in Bunyan’s book and with The Preacher’s: “All is vanity and a striving after wind.” There must be some connection between Bunyan, the Bible, and Thackeray. This connection appears very striking in Thackeray’s epilogue to “Vanity Fair”, where he says: “Ah! Vanitas Vanitatum! which of us is happy in this world? Which of us has his desire? or, having it, is satisfied? - Come, children, let us shut up the box and the puppets, for our play is played out.” After reading this, and with the whole impression of the novel “Vanity Fair” still fresh, it is very easy to bring lo mind those words of The Preacher, which Bunyan refers to in his description of his Vanity Fair: “Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher; vanity of vanities, all is vanity . . . I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and, behold, all is vanity and a striving after wind . . . ’) The impression is still more intensified by reading Bunyan himself in his suggestive de- scription of the arrival of Christian and Faithful at Vanity Fair: “Then I saw in my Dream, that when they were got out of the wil- derness, they presently saw a Town before them, and the name of that town is Vanity; and at the Town there is a Fair kept called Vanity-Fair, it is kept all the year long, it beareth the name of Vanity Fair, because the Town where it is kept is lighter than Vanity; and also, because all that is there sold, or that cometh thither, is l) Melville 1, p. 231 sq. (London 1927). *) E. Walter: Entstehungsgeschichte von W. M. Thackerays ’Vanity Fair”, in ”) The Pr. 1 : 2, 1 : 14, 2 : 11, 17 (Holy Bible). Palaestra 79, Berlin 1908, p. 1 sq.

VANITY PAIR 79 Vanity. As is the saying of the wise, all that cometh is Vanity. (Isa. 40. 7. Eccles. I. ch. 2, 11, 17)” ’). The impression of the accordance between the Bible, Bunyan, and Thackeray is therefore not accidental. What is clear to any attentive reader, can be supported by a tract which, so far as I know, has not been considered. At about the same time as Thackeray was born, an excerpt was printed from Runyan’s “The Pilgrim’s Progress” with the title “Vanity Fair, and the Trial and Death of Faithful From the Pilgrim’s Progress” *). It is not impossible that Thackeray may have read this booklet in his youth - 8 pages in length - which describes the fair of vanity in this world. Apart from that, it is clear that the separate publication of the description of Vanity Fair proves that this part of Runyan’s book must have been particularly popular. The interest in Bunyan’s account of the fair of vanity seems to have been specially vivid at that time. Generally, it may be said about the efforts of the translators of different countries to find an adequate phrase for Thacheray’s book- title “Vanity Fair”, that that translation must be the best which most clearly expresses the general tendency and contents of the book, deriving its name from Bunyan’s Vanity Fair in the Town of Vanity. In this way the difficulty of the translation is solved for all languages. We have already pointed out, how nearly related Bunyan is to The Preacher. His diction and his choice of words in the description of the fair of vanity is partially the same as The Preacher’s. The translators need only borrow the phraseology of the latter from such translations l ) J. Bunyan, The Pilgrim’s Progress, ed. by J. Brown, Cambridge 1907, p. 213. Besides, Thackeray has told us himself what he aimed at with his book Vanity Fair. His daughter relates in the prefacc to her edition of Vanity Fair, in 1906, the following: “My father has left his own criticisms of “Vanity Fair” . . .: “What I want is to make a set of people living without God in the World (only that is a cant phrase), greedy, pompous men, perfectly self-satisfied for the most part, and at ease about their superior virtue . . .” (Introduction to Vanity Fair by his daughter Anne Ritchie, London 1906, p. XXXVI sq.) *) J. Bunyan: Vanity Fair, and the Trial and Death of Faithful From the Pil- grim’s Progress. pp. 8. T. Williams (London 18101) 8:o. (Cottage Library of Christian Knowledge. The German translations mentioned above are in this respect of especial interest. Present circiimstances have prevented me from in- vestigating the reasons which the German translators may perhaps have given to support their interpretations, and I must pass them over for the present. But the translations of my own country are not less interesting, because here an erroneous interpretation of Thacke- ray’s title has been carried over from the first Swedish translation to the last I ) . Both Bolin, Sommarstriim, and Lange have turned the title “Vanity Fair” into Swedish by the words “Flfangans marknad”, whereas Backman calls his translation “Varldsmarknaden” *). In his introduction, Backman shows that he feels some of the atmosphere of “vanitas vanitatum” in “Vanity Fair”, when he says: “Few poets have with more delicacy and truth than Thackeray brought out the importance of the time factor, the changing of the characters under the stress of events and in the course of the years. Underlying the whole story is the idea of “vanitas vanitatum”, the fugitiveness of everything. This gives to his work a deep perspective, a touch of the tragedy of history . . .” ’) This knowledge did not, however, prevent him from translating the title by the commonplace word ”VHrlds- marknaden”, which still less than the title “Flfangans marknad” has anything in common with the words and the spirit of The Preacher, as it appears in Thackeray’s novel. From the earliest Swedish version of the Bible to the present one, The Preacher’s “vanitas vanitatum” has been translated by “Flfang- ligheternas FBfanglighet”. The word “fManglighet”, therefore, has in Swedish exactly the same sense as the Latin “vanitas”, and above all, it calls up the same associations. Translated into English, it covers the same idea as ”vanity”. The word “flfanga” preferred by the translators has on the other hand partially - but only partially - ~~ I) See translations of Thackeray’s Vanity Fair, 1849 by N. L. VANITY FAIR 81 the same sense as “fifanglighet” l ) , but has never been employed in the Biblical sense. It means about the same as the Engl. ‘‘conceit’’ or “priue”. On the other hand, the Swedish translators of Bunyan have loyally translated his “The Town of Vanity” by the Biblical expres- sion “Staden FHfanglighet”, and his “Vanity Fair” by “FHfanglig- hetens marknad”, which is quite correct. Only in the most modern Swedish translations of Bunyan’s “The Pilgrim’s Progress”, have they begun to translate “Vanity Fair” by the inadequate expression “FA- fangps marknad”, varying with the correct one. Very likely, this is due to influence from the inadequate translations of Thackeray: “ FHfangans marknad”, which seems to have influenced linguistic usage to such a degree, that it is has now in the Swedish language hecome a household word for all sorts of vainness, emptiness and fugitiveness *). It is not easy to say from where the first translator of Thackeray’s “Vanity Fair” in Sweden, Bolin, got his expression “FH- fRngans marknad”. Surely the connection between the Bible, Bunyan, and Thackeray, cannot have been quite clear to him. The other Swe- dish translators, perhaps, have followed him without deeper reflection. The translation “Varldsmarknaden” may have been influenced by the German interpretation “Jahrmarkt des Lebens” ’). None of the two expressions have any support in Swedish Bible versions. They are everyday words, without anything of the mighty knowledge of the world, which speaks out of The Preacher.
